summary: A 1978 specification of JANUS, a symmetrical, 1822-like interface for the Packet Radio project to connect radio units to other equipment. It is related to BBN Report 1822 for the ARPANET.

plainLanguage.summary: A plug standard where both sides are the same kind of device. It was meant for radio network units.

questions: why do network interfaces need symmetry
subtitle: A symmetrical electrical and protocol interface for connecting network devices

tldr.problem: The 1822 interface (which connects hosts to ARPANET IMPs) was asymmetrical: some aspects were specific to the IMP side and others to the host side. This made it impossible for two 1822-compatible devices to connect to each other directly.
tldr.mechanism: JANUS respecifies the 1822 interface to be fully symmetrical: both sides use identical handshakes, timing, electrical levels, and protocols. It defines low-level requirements (four-way handshake, message padding, timing tolerances) and distant-host electrical specifications (RS-422 differential signaling and optical isolation).
tldr.outcome: Any two devices with JANUS interfaces can connect to each other, enabling packet radio units and other equipment to talk directly without requiring a central switching node.

today: JANUS was designed for the Packet Radio project and represents an early experiment in symmetrical network interfaces. While the specific interface is not in use today, its principles influenced later standards for peer-to-peer device communication. The concept of symmetrical electrical and protocol specifications remains important in modern networking standards.

sections.title: The Problem with 1822
sections.content:
The 1822 interface connects ARPANET hosts to IMPs. Report 1822 states that "the technique of transferring information between the Host and the IMP is identical in each direction," suggesting symmetry. However, in practice some aspects are specific to the IMP and others to the host, breaking true interchangeability.

The Packet Radio project needed an interface where two devices could connect directly to each other for peer-to-peer communication. JANUS fixes this by removing all asymmetry from 1822, creating a fully symmetrical interface suitable for pairing any two devices—including Packet Radio units, multiplexors, and front ends.
sections.plainLanguage: The old plug was designed for a host to plug into an IMP, with one side special and the other special. To connect two hosts or two radios together, you need both sides to be identical.

sections.title: JANUS Specifications
sections.content:
JANUS covers two areas: low-level protocol and distant-host electrical requirements. Low-level protocol aspects—padding, message length, handshaking, timing, and signal deskewing—can be implemented in hardware, software, or both.

The interface requires padding received messages to full word length with zeros; accepts messages up to 8160 bits (allowing flexibility for non-ARPANET applications); uses a four-way handshake for reliability (two-way handshakes are forbidden due to deadlock risks); and enforces timing constraints such as a 1/10-second delay after raising the Ready relay to prevent contact bounce.
sections.plainLanguage: The spec says how fast signals must transition, how long they must stay on or off, how messages are padded, and how long to wait before sending data after turning on a relay.

sections.title: Electrical Requirements
sections.content:
For distant-host connections, JANUS specifies RS-422 differential signaling (2 to 6 volts output, 0.2 volts minimum input sensitivity) and optical isolation to handle large common-mode voltage differences. The receiver must operate correctly over ±100 volts common-mode voltage and must not be permanently damaged by ±300 volts.

These specifications replace the transformer coupling and strict rise-time requirements of 1822, enabling more robust communication over longer distances and with greater tolerance for ground potential differences between devices.
sections.plainLanguage: When devices are far apart, use special cables that send signals as voltage differences rather than absolute levels, and put optical isolators in between so that ground potential differences do not cause problems.

sections.title: Scope and Limitations
sections.content:
JANUS defines the electrical interface but deliberately leaves high-level software protocols to the application, since the interface serves many applications beyond ARPANET connectivity. JANUS does not specify how to form connections, negotiate options, or exchange messages above the hardware level.

While JANUS itself is fully symmetrical, a JANUS-equipped device communicating with the ARPANET through an IMP will still see the marker bit appended by the source IMP, since IMPs themselves remain asymmetrical. This does not affect JANUS-to-JANUS communication between two devices not involving the ARPANET.
sections.plainLanguage: JANUS says what plugs and wires look like, not what messages mean. Each application defines its own message types. And if you plug a JANUS device into an IMP, you still get the IMP's quirks.
